title: Docker logs crashes every couple of hours
body: Every couple of hours, `docker compose logs` crashes on two production AWS EC2 environments. The daemon log first contains an unmarshalling error such as `proto: LogEntry: illegal tag 0 (wire type 6)`, followed by `log message is too large` errors claiming messages are nearly 2 GB. Running `docker logs` for the affected time range produces the same error, and cached local logs can miss hours that are present in CloudWatch. Both environments use the `awslogs` driver and Docker Engine 20.10.23; one runs Kong/nginx and the other runs a Node.js application beside nginx. I could not identify an unusual application log entry or reproduce the problem in a dummy container.

symptoms_visible: Every few hours `docker compose logs` exits after an `error unmarshalling log entry` message and repeated `log message is too large` errors claiming a message is nearly 2 GB.
Running `docker logs` over the affected interval gives the same error, and the local cached output can omit hours of entries that I can still see in CloudWatch.
N0.label: N0 periodic local log read failure reported

symptoms_visible: The unmarshalling and oversized-message errors still occur on the Amazon Linux instances.
I also see a similar oversized-message failure when reading rotated local-driver logs on a non-AWS machine.
N1.label: N1 distribution patch and cross-environment evidence collected

symptoms_visible: After temporarily switching the affected container from `awslogs` to `local`, `docker compose logs` was still running and the instance was healthy about twenty hours later; manual `docker logs` showed the local entries.
N2.label: N2 logging-driver probe completed

symptoms_visible: The recent container log files look binary when I open them with `less`; I sent an affected set privately for inspection.
N3.label: N3 affected local cache supplied

symptoms_visible: All of my environments are currently reporting healthy after automatic AWS server updates, even though I did not change the application stacks or the `awslogs` logging configuration.
N4.label: N4 environments healthy after automatic platform update

symptoms_visible: After updating to a Moby release containing the resilient local-log reader, `docker logs` moves past a damaged log file instead of repeatedly terminating with unmarshalling or implausibly large-message errors.
N_terminal.label: terminal local log reader recovers from corruption

question_patterns: Can you inspect the Amazon Linux Docker source RPM and confirm which downstream logging patches are present?
Please run the SRPM extraction commands and paste the logging-related patch names.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran the same commands on my instance. The extracted SRPM includes `docker-20.10.4-Limit-logger-errors-logged-into-daemon-logs.patch`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The installed package is an unmodified upstream Moby build and the SRPM contains no Amazon logging patches.
The same patch is present, but the package revision is a slightly newer Amazon Linux build.

question_patterns: Does this only happen on Amazon Linux with `awslogs`, or has anyone reproduced a similar read failure elsewhere?
Are there affected systems using the local driver outside AWS?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I also have an affected Ubuntu 20.04-based VM on IBM Cloud using the `local` driver with compressed 20 MB rotation. `docker logs` ends with `log message is too large`, and the latest logs are lost, although I did not capture the same unmarshalling line there.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: No — every affected system uses the same Amazon Linux package and `awslogs`; an upstream build with the local driver never shows the error.

edges.comment: The Amazon patch confirmation comes from the reporter. The non-AWS local-driver case comes from a second affected user and is folded into the simulated user side. Together these facts show that the Amazon patch can alter error reporting but is not sufficient to explain every oversized-length read failure.

question_patterns: Can you temporarily switch one frequently affected container from `awslogs` to `local` and report whether the log-reading error recurs?
Please run a controlled logging-driver comparison on the instance that normally fails within a few hours.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I switched the driver from `awslogs` to `local`. After about twenty hours, `docker compose logs` was still running and the instance was still healthy. I also ran `docker logs` manually and the logs were all there.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same unmarshalling and oversized-message errors returned within two hours while using only the local driver.
It stayed healthy for eighteen hours instead of twenty, with the same successful manual log read.

edges.comment: This handler-initiated logging-driver toggle is a diagnostic measurement, even though using `local` temporarily avoided the reporter's frequent failure. It does not establish an awslogs encoding mismatch as the root cause, particularly because another user saw corrupted-length behavior with the local driver.

question_patterns: Can you provide the affected files from `/var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/local-logs` for inspection?
Please preserve and share a container log file from an occurrence, if its contents can be shared safely.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I made a fresh export from an environment that had the issue and sent the Docker container logs to the email address on your GitHub profile.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I cannot provide an affected file, and all retained local log files decode normally with no damaged region.

question_patterns: What do the retained local log files look like when you inspect them directly?
Do basic tools treat the affected cache as ordinary text or binary data?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The recent files look weird, and `less` considers them binary files.

edges.comment: The files were delivered privately, so no attachment path is referenced. The user reports only what they observed and sent; interpreting the record framing and corruption is engineer-side analysis.

question_patterns: What Elastic Beanstalk platform version are the now-healthy instances running?
Can you check whether an automatic platform or Docker package update occurred?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: My environments are all on `Docker running on 64bit Amazon Linux 2/3.7.1` now. We have automatic updates enabled on the AWS servers.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: There were no operating-system, platform, Docker, or package updates between the failing and healthy periods.

question_patterns: Did you change the application stack or logging mechanism before the environments became healthy?
Is `awslogs` still configured on the healthy environments?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Nothing changed on our side as far as I know. We did not update our application stacks or change the logging mechanism; `awslogs` started working again after the automatic server updates.

edges.comment: This records the later persistent platform update as a new system state. The temporary healthy period is not proof that the corrupted-log-reader defect was fixed, because no relevant Moby logging-code change was identified at that time.

solution.intent: Treat the huge message size as a corrupted local-log framing value, recover existing installations by removing or avoiding the damaged file, and update to Moby 27.4.0 or newer so the local-log reader skips the rest of a file after a decoding failure instead of aborting the whole log stream.
solution.concrete_example: The local format is `[message length][protobuf message][message length]`. Once a partial or corrupted write destroys that framing, the reader can interpret bytes from the damaged region as a multi-gigabyte length and cannot recover in older releases. Delete the affected local log file if immediate recovery is required, or scope `docker logs` with `--since`, `--until`, or `--tail` so it does not include that file. Then upgrade to Moby 27.4.0+ or v28, where PR #47983 makes the reader skip the remainder of a file after a decode failure. Please retest `docker logs` and `docker compose logs` on the updated engine and confirm that later files remain readable before declaring the incident resolved.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied raw errors and affected files but did not identify the framing mechanism. Engineering determined that local records use length/protobuf/length framing, that corruption can make message bytes look like an enormous length, and that sudden shutdowns can leave incomplete writes or null-filled regions, particularly with metadata-only journaling. PR #47983 changed the reader to abandon the damaged remainder and continue with the next file; it shipped in Moby v28 and was backported to v27.4.0 and newer.

edges.comment: Final resolution from the maintainer's March 2024 and May 2025 analyses. The Amazon rate-limiting patch and the proposed awslogs/local encoding mismatch were intermediate hypotheses, not the general root cause. Verification is requested terminal-side because the reporter did not retest the later landed fix in the thread.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the direct cause as corruption of the local log file's length/protobuf framing: after synchronization is lost, older readers interpret damaged bytes as an implausibly large message length and cannot recover.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence, including the protobuf unmarshalling error, multi-gigabyte reported lengths, damaged local cache, and a similar failure outside the original Amazon awslogs setup.

Must not present the Amazon `Limit-logger-errors-logged-into-daemon-logs` patch or an awslogs/local encoding mismatch as the general root cause; those were intermediate theories and do not explain the non-AWS local-driver case.

Must recommend updating to a Moby release containing the resilient local-log reader, which skips the remainder of a corrupt file and continues; deleting the existing damaged file or excluding it with `--since`, `--until`, or `--tail` may be offered as recovery for old data.
Must ask the user to verify `docker logs` or `docker compose logs` on an engine containing the resilient-reader fix before treating the issue as resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Production operator with moderate Docker and AWS experience; comfortable running package-inspection commands, changing logging drivers for a controlled test, inspecting container files, and supplying private diagnostic data, but explicitly defers on Docker's binary log internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, cautious, and cooperative; reports exact commands and errors, distinguishes observations from speculation, avoids risky rebuilds on production, and follows up after extended monitoring.
